subject: Chemistry
title: Cochineal Red: Color From Bugs
description: A micro-lesson that makes Cochineal Red: Color From Bugs usable.

hook.text: The bright red in your Starbucks drink may come from crushed insects. Cochineal dye is made from scale bugs.

buildup.text: Cochineal insects live on cactus in Central America. They produce carminic acid to repel predators.

discovery.text: Crushing 70,000 dried insects yields one pound of dye. The Aztecs valued it almost as highly as gold.

twist.text: After Spain conquered the Aztecs, cochineal became the most valuable export after silver. A color funded an empire.

climax.text: Cochineal is still used in food (E120), cosmetics, and fabric. It's one of the safest red dyes known.

punchline.text: Crushed bugs make brilliant red. Still in your food, lipstick, and drinks.

quiz.question: What produces the red color in cochineal dye?
options: Carminic acid from crushed scale insects on cactus plants
Iron oxide extracted from desert sand
A synthetic pigment invented by Spanish chemists

details.summary: Cochineal red, or carmine, is extracted from the crushed bodies of Dactylopius coccus scale insects that live on prickly pear cacti in the Americas. The pigment molecule carminic acid produces a vivid red used in food, cosmetics, and textiles for over a thousand years.
details.whyItMatters: Cochineal was colonial Mexico's second most valuable export after silver. It remains widely used today as a natural food colorant listed as E120, appearing in yogurt, candy, and cosmetics.
takeaways: Carminic acid from crushed scale insects produces a vivid red dye
Cochineal was more valuable than gold per ounce in colonial trade
It is still used as natural food colorant E120 in modern products

faq.question: How many insects are needed to produce a usable amount of cochineal dye?
faq.answer: Approximately seventy thousand dried cochineal insects produce one pound of dye. Harvesting is labor-intensive, requiring workers to brush the tiny insects from cactus pads by hand. This enormous insect-to-dye ratio makes natural cochineal relatively expensive.

faq.question: Why does cochineal labeling on food products cause consumer concern?
faq.answer: Many consumers are uncomfortable eating insect-derived colorants. Vegans and those with insect allergies avoid cochineal products. Some religions have dietary restrictions regarding insects. Food labeling now requires explicit mention of cochineal or carmine rather than vague terms.
